label: Kimi K3.1 Pro
output:
Peckham, London  
[Date]

Kelechi Obi  
Croydon  
London

Dear Kelechi,

Well, here it is. A proper letter, typed, printed, put in an envelope and posted to Croydon, because you decided a voice note was not serious enough. I hope you’re reading this on the train, as promised. If somebody is looking over your shoulder, leave them. I need witnesses.

You spent a suspiciously large part of my birthday complaining about your job. Nine years as a quantity surveyor and, according to you, every day has become the same spreadsheet with a different date on it. Then I suggested teaching maths and you laughed — properly laughed — before saying that if I was serious, I should put it in writing.

So, K, I’m serious.

Not “I’ve had an idea, so I’m going to harass you about it until Christmas” serious. Serious enough to explain properly why I think you should at least look into it, and serious enough to tell you the bad parts too.

First, forget whether you can imagine yourself standing in front of a classroom. Just think about what I’ve actually seen you do.

You got an A in further maths. You were also the person tutoring half our hostel in Moremi before exams. People didn’t come to you just because you knew the answers. They came because you could take something that looked impossible, break it down and explain it without making them feel stupid. You were patient with people, even when they were asking you the same question for the third time and your own revision was waiting.

And before you say that was university and these are children, remember what you did with my nephew at Christmas. You taught him fractions using portions of jollof rice on plates. No big announcement, no performance. You just found a way to make it make sense. The boy still talks about it.

You’re funny, you’re patient, and you can explain things without showing off. Those things matter more than you realise. Children know very quickly when an adult is making them feel foolish. They also know when somebody is genuinely trying to help them understand.

At my school in Peckham — 1,100 children, before you think this is some tiny little operation — we’ve had a supply teacher covering two Year 9 maths groups since September. I’m not saying you could walk in tomorrow and solve everything, and I’m not trying to emotionally blackmail you with Year 9. But when I walk past those classrooms and then listen to you saying you’re bored to death at work, it’s difficult not to put the two things together.

Last month, I finally got through to a Year 11 boy called Damola on simultaneous equations. We’d been at it for three weeks. Three weeks of him looking at the page as if I had personally invented algebra to ruin his life. Then it clicked, and he suddenly shouted, “Is that all??” The whole class clapped.

I laughed so much I nearly lost my place in the lesson.

That’s the thing. For him, it wasn’t just two equations. It was three weeks of thinking he couldn’t do something, followed by the discovery that he could. You don’t get that moment every day. Sometimes you get it after a lot of repetition, a lot of frustration and a lot of wondering whether anything you’re saying is entering anybody’s head. But when it comes, it’s real.

Now the part I would hide if I were trying to recruit you with a glossy leaflet.

Teaching is hard. The marking is endless. Behaviour some days is pure wahala. You can spend ages planning a lesson, then watch it get derailed by an argument over a pen. There are emails, meetings, parents’ evenings, observations and days when you’ll go home wondering why anybody willingly does this.

You will not be brilliant immediately just because you know maths and children might like you. You’ll have to learn classroom management, how to pace a lesson, what to challenge and what to ignore. Some children will test you simply because you’re new. I won’t insult your intelligence by pretending otherwise.

When I started in 2019, I cried in the car park twice in my first term. Not almost cried. Cried. Sat in the car and questioned my whole decision. The days were long, everything was new, and I thought I should somehow be good at it immediately.

It got better. Not perfect — better. I learned routines. I stopped trying to do everything at once. I learned which battles were worth having and how to recover when a lesson went sideways. Now the difficult days are still difficult, but they don’t make me feel like the whole job is impossible.

There’s the money too. Yes, there would be a pay drop in your first year. I’m not going to mumble that part and start talking about holidays. The salaried training route means you’d be paid while you train, and it takes one year, starting in September 2027. So this isn’t “resign tomorrow and survive on vibes.” But you should still look at the actual figures carefully before making any decision.

The holidays and pension are part of the package, and the pay goes up. The holidays are not entirely work-free, despite what people outside teaching like to announce on social media. Even so, they make a real difference. We can sit down and compare everything properly. You can put the numbers into one of your beloved spreadsheets and interrogate them until they confess.

And please don’t start that “I’m too old” business at 34. A woman in my department started at 41. You would not be arriving as some ancient relic. Your nine years of work experience wouldn’t disappear either. You understand deadlines, responsibility, professionalism and how numbers are used outside a textbook. All of that would come with you.

Honestly, Kelechi, sometimes I think you’re wasting yourself checking other people’s costings. Not because quantity surveying is beneath you, and not because the last nine years have been useless. I mean that there’s a whole part of you — the part that taught half of Moremi, the part that used jollof rice to explain fractions — sitting there unused while you complete another spreadsheet.

On your last birthday, you said, “I just want to do something that matters before 40.” You can pretend you were just making conversation if you like, but I remembered it.

I’m not holding you hostage to one birthday sentence, and I’m not promising that teaching will definitely make you happy. Nobody sensible could promise that. I’m saying there might be something here worth investigating, and you are better placed for it than you think.

So this is the actual ask. No dramatic career change this week. No application while you’re standing at the station. No signature on anything.

Come to the open evening at the training partnership in Lewisham on Thursday 19 November 2026 at 6pm. I’ll come with you.

Ask them annoying questions. Ask exactly what the salary is, what support trainees get, what the workload is really like, where you might be placed and what happens when you have a terrible day. Bring your quantity-surveyor suspicion and examine everything. If it sounds rubbish, we’ll leave and you can tell me you were right.

Applications for September 2027 open soon, so it’s worth finding out now rather than leaving it until the decision has practically made itself. One evening is not a commitment. It’s information.

And if you go, ask your questions and still decide it’s not for you, I’ll drop it. You can continue your life of costings in peace — at least until the next time you start moaning about spreadsheets at somebody’s birthday.

You laughed and told me to put it in writing. I’ve done that. Now you have no excuse, abeg.

One evening. That’s all.

Your guy,

[Your name]

P.S. Yes, I actually posted this. And no, you cannot reply with a nine-minute voice note. A simple “Fine, I’ll come” will do.
